title: Maitreyi's question and the breath of the Vedas
hook: Maitreyi turns down a fortune to ask what doesn't die, and hears where the Vedas come from.
carry: the vedas are shruti: heard, breathed out by brahman
tomorrow: a young monk, a ritual master, two garlands. whose wilts first?

segments.voice: Yesterday, jnana as a search: Bhrigu looked again and again until he saw Brahman for himself. Today, the third sutra, and a woman who turned down a fortune.

The sage Yajnavalkya is about to leave home life behind. He has two wives, Maitreyi and Katyayani, and he offers to settle his property between them before he goes. Maitreyi stops him. If this whole earth, full of wealth, were mine, she asks, would it make me immortal? No, he says. You'd live the way rich people live. That's all. Then what would I do with something that won't make me immortal? Tell me what you know. So he does. And in the middle of that teaching, he says where the Vedas come from.
screen: `SPLIT THE FORTUNE?` → `WOULD IT MAKE ME IMMORTAL?` → `TELL ME WHAT YOU KNOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, in paraphrase: as smoke billows from a fire of damp wood, so the Rig Veda and the other Vedas are the breathing out of this great being. That's the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, and it sits under one of Hinduism's central beliefs. The Vedas are shruti, which means what was heard. Much of the tradition holds that no human sat down and composed them. The ancient rishis heard them, and passed them on mouth to ear for many centuries. That's why a priest at a wedding or a thread ceremony chants Vedic verses exactly, sound by sound: the words are treated as received, not invented. The third sutra builds on this. Shastra yonitvat. Shastra is scripture; yoni is source. Shankara reads it two ways and keeps both. Brahman is the source of scripture, breathing it out without effort. And scripture is the source of knowing Brahman, which reasoning alone can't reach. Out, and back again. So in Shankara's school, the path of jnana starts with listening: hearing the Upanishads from a teacher, reflecting on them, then dwelling on them until they're one's own. Maitreyi did exactly that. She set down a fortune and asked to hear. Other schools weigh scripture and reasoning differently, and they've argued it out with care.
screen: `THE VEDAS, BREATHED OUT.` · `SHRUTI: WHAT WAS HEARD.` · `THE THIRD SUTRA: SHASTRA YONITVAT.` · `OUT, AND BACK AGAIN.` · then, large: `SHE ASKED TO HEAR.`

segments.voice: If your family has a prayer or a mantra, say it once, slowly, aloud or under your breath, and listen to each sound as something handed down to you, not made up by you. If you don't pray, sit tall with your hands open and let three out-breaths leave without pushing, the way the Upanishad pictures the Vedas, breathed out.
Jnana: knowledge that frees. In the third sutra, it starts with listening: scripture flows out of Brahman, and leads back to knowing it.
Pocket this, from Maitreyi's teacher: the Vedas are shruti, heard, breathed out by Brahman. Back here tomorrow.

howItsDone: Vedic verses are still learned by ear, teacher to student, and chanted with exact sounds at rites like weddings and the thread ceremony; in Advaita Vedanta, students come to knowledge of Brahman through hearing the Upanishads from a teacher (shravana), reflecting on them (manana) and dwelling on them deeply (nididhyasana).
